The Feature Article

READ FIRST
Listen to the articleListen and follow the highlighted sentence. Voice availability depends on your browser.

How Tamales Are Made: An Ancient Recipe

Long before there were stoves, supermarkets, or even the word “Mexico,” people in Mesoamerica were wrapping corn dough around a filling and cooking it in the leaves the harvest left behind. Tamales have roots stretching back thousands of years, making them one of the oldest prepared foods still eaten today. Aztec and Maya cooks carried them to markets, offered them in ceremonies, and packed them for soldiers on the march — the tamal was an early portable meal.

The process has barely changed across generations, and it follows a careful order. First, the cook soaks dried corn husks in warm water until they become soft and flexible. A dry husk cracks; a soaked one folds like cloth. Next, the cook prepares the masa, beating corn dough with broth and fat until it turns smooth and fluffy. Experienced cooks say the masa is ready when a small piece floats in a glass of water. Then comes the assembly: the cook spreads a thin layer of masa across each husk, leaving the edges bare. After that, a spoonful of filling — pork in red chile, chicken in green salsa, beans, cheese, even sweet pineapple — goes down the center, and the husk is folded closed around it like an envelope. Finally, the tamales stand upright in a steamer pot, where hot vapor cooks them slowly for about an hour. No oil, no oven — just steam, a method with deep roots in Mesoamerican cooking.

What makes the order matter is chemistry as much as tradition. Skip the soaking, and the husks tear. Rush the masa, and the tamales turn out dense instead of light. Open the steamer too early, and the dough stays sticky. Every step prepares the ingredients for the step that follows — which is why, in kitchens from Oaxaca to Mississippi, the recipe is passed down not as a list of ingredients but as a sequence of actions, taught hand over hand at a family table. A tamalada, the gathering where families make tamales together by the dozen, is really a classroom: the elders run the masa station, the children learn to spread and fold, and the recipe survives another generation.

🌽 Quick Glossary

masa — corn dough, the base of a tamal · husk — corn leaf used as a wrapper (hoja de maíz) · flexible — able to bend without breaking · vapor — water in gas form; steam · dense — heavy and packed tight · tamalada — a tamal-making gathering

My Tamale Guide

Your assignment: Create a one-page illustrated guide that teaches someone how tamales are made. Write in your own words. Use the article for evidence.

Open writing support

Start here: Write one short sentence for each step. Use First, Next, Then, After that, Finally.
Explain: “This step matters because ___.”
Use evidence: “The article says, ‘___.’ This supports my explanation because ___.”
Connect: “A tamalada helps people ___.”
Go further: Include precise verbs, vocabulary such as flexible or masa, and explain a cause-and-effect relationship.

Your illustration

Draw one part of the process, or upload a photograph of your own drawing. Add a caption that explains it.
